lead: Little Rock sits on the Arkansas River where the Ozark foothills meet the delta. Tornadoes, river floods and heavy storms cause most of its water damage.
risk: tornado and storm damage, river flooding and flash floods
why: On March 31, 2023, a strong tornado cut across west Little Rock and into North Little Rock. It damaged or destroyed hundreds of homes and businesses along its path, and many roofs were torn open. Rain fell into exposed rooms in the days that followed. Spring storms bring hail and high winds most years too, and even a near miss can drop trees on roofs across the city.

Flooding comes from the river and from local creeks. In 2019, the Arkansas River ran at record or near-record levels for weeks, flooding low areas along its banks. In Little Rock itself, heavy rain fills Fourche Creek, Coleman Creek and other streams fast. About 53% of homes were built before 1980, and older roofs, drains and supply lines add everyday risk.
image_alt: Aerial view of tornado damage with roofs torn off and power lines down
image_caption: Spring storms and tornadoes can tear open Little Rock roofs.
problems: West Little Rock and wooded areas
Homes near Fourche and Coleman creeks
Pre-1980 homes in Hillcrest, the Heights
tips: Have a plan and a safe room for tornado warnings.
Tarp a damaged roof fast to stop more rain from getting in.
Check the flood map if you live near a creek or the river.
Take photos of every room before storm season for your claim.
areas: Calls come from Hillcrest, the Heights, the Quapaw Quarter, SoMa, Pleasant Valley, Chenal Valley, Capitol View and Riverdale, plus North Little Rock, Sherwood and Maumelle.

faq.q: What should I do first after a storm damages my Little Rock roof?
faq.a: Make sure everyone is safe and stay away from downed lines. Take photos, then get the roof tarped to keep more rain out. Call your insurer and start a claim. DryFlare can dry the attic, ceilings and walls so mold does not set in while repairs are planned.
